source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb (and glossary); 8.5

main.t: A small pea-shaped bone on the front of the triquetrum, at the base of the hand (pisiform).

simpler.t: The pisiform is the small round wrist bone at the base of your palm, on the little-finger side.

deeper.t: It sits on the front of the triquetrum, not in line with the other bones of its row.

facts.t: It is the fourth bone of the first row, counting from the thumb side.
Unlike the rest of its row, it sits on the front (anterior) surface of the triquetrum.
From there it projects forwards, forming the bump at the inner base of the hand.

simpler.t: Feel the bump at the base of your palm, below the little finger: that is the pisiform.

deeper.t: Its only joint is with the triquetrum.

items.name: Facet for the triquetrum
items.t: A flat surface on its back, where it meets the triquetrum.

items.name: Front surface
items.t: Projects forwards, so you can feel it at the base of the hand.

items.name: Attachment of the flexor retinaculum
items.t: The inner end of the flexor retinaculum anchors to it.

simpler.t: It is a small round bone that you can feel through the skin.

deeper.t: It lies within the tendon of a forearm muscle (flexor carpi ulnaris), like a kneecap within its tendon.

facts.t: It anchors the inner end of the flexor retinaculum, which holds the carpal bones in their U shape.
It is the only carpal bone out of line with its row: it sits on the triquetrum.

simpler.t: The pisiform anchors the band that roofs the carpal tunnel.

items.name: Triquetrum
items.t: Its only joint: it sits on the triquetrum’s front surface.

items.name: Flexor retinaculum
items.t: Attached on the little-finger side to the hamate and pisiform.

items.name: Carpal tunnel
items.t: The flexor retinaculum it anchors forms the roof of the tunnel.

items.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
items.t: Its tendon attaches to the pisiform.

items.name: Ulnar nerve and artery
items.t: Pass beside it into the hand, outside the carpal tunnel.

simpler.t: It sits on the triquetrum and anchors the roof of the carpal tunnel.

facts.t: It forms by replacing a cartilage model with bone (endochondral ossification), like all limb bones except the clavicle.
Its single ossification centre appears last of the carpal bones, at about the twelfth year.
facts.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20). Gray’s 1918 (8.2) gives about the twelfth year (supporting only).

items.injury: A fall onto the heel of the hand on the little-finger side.
items.cannotDo: Bend the wrist towards the little-finger side without pain.
items.why: A forearm muscle tendon attaches to it and pulls on the broken bone.

items.injury: Long pressure on the base of the palm, as in long-distance cycling.
items.damaged: The ulnar nerve beside the pisiform.
items.cannotDo: Spread and close the fingers strongly; the little finger may feel numb.
items.why: The nerve passes beside the pisiform and the hook of the hamate into the hand.

items.q: Explain why you can feel the pisiform when you cannot feel most carpal bones.
model: It sits on the front of the triquetrum, not in line with its row.
So it forms a bump at the inner base of the hand.
Most carpal bones lie deeper, in their two rows.

items.q: Compare the pisiform and the hook of the hamate.
model: Both are on the little-finger side of the hand.
The pisiform is a whole bone sitting on the triquetrum.
The hook is a bony extension on the front of the hamate.
The flexor retinaculum attaches on this side to the hamate and pisiform.

items.q: After a long ride, a cyclist’s little finger feels numb. Predict the nerve affected and where.
model: It is pressed where it passes beside the pisiform into the hand.
The pressure comes from leaning on the handlebars.
The median nerve, in the carpal tunnel, is spared.

check.stem: Which bone does the pisiform sit on?
check.why: It sits on the front surface of the triquetrum.
The flexor retinaculum attaches medially to the hamate and pisiform.
